summary: A document submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550, discussing hosts that have many addresses. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A note about what happens when one computer has lots of different addresses.

questions: why would a host need many ip addresses
can a computer have multiple addresses
subtitle: Why and how hosts can use many IP addresses at once.

tldr.problem: Hosts have traditionally had one IP address, but multiple useful scenarios—offering different services, managing costs, and enabling mobility—suggest hosts should have many addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explores several use cases where a single host benefits from multiple addresses: encoding services, accounting for usage-sensitive billing, allocating addresses to individual users, enabling subnet mobility, and allowing hosts to bridge multiple logical networks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends reserving 2^6 to 2^8 (64 to 256) extra addresses per host in address-space planning, but the idea remained largely theoretical and was not widely adopted in practice.

today: RFC 1681 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. The proposal to use many addresses per host was not widely adopted. IPv4 address scarcity and the eventual transition to IPv6 changed the landscape of how addresses are used.

sections.title: Multiple Addresses per Host
sections.content:
Most hosts on the Internet have had a single IP address. Steven Bellovin argues this assumption may change. He proposes that hosts should be able to have many addresses, each useful for a different purpose, and that network planners should reserve address space to accommodate this.

Bellovin notes the idea is plausible and expects many of the schemes he describes will be tried, even if multiple addresses are not the only or best way to solve each problem.
sections.eli5: A computer usually has one address, but what if it needed lots of them, each for a different reason?

sections.title: Use Cases for Multiple Addresses
sections.content:
Several practical scenarios motivate the need for multiple addresses on a single host:

Service encoding: Different services can advertise different addresses on the same machine. For example, one address could serve files via FTP while another runs Archie or another protocol. This avoids requiring users to remember custom ports or host names and provides security benefits: a firewall can grant access to one address while blocking others on the same machine.

Billing and accounting: Encoding charge policies in the IP address itself allows routers to enforce usage-sensitive billing schemes without consulting a service. Users avoid surprise charges, and different user classes can have different privileges based on address bits.

Per-user addresses: Assigning each user on a host a separate IP address during their login session enables per-user accounting at the router level and allows encryption policies to protect individual users rather than whole hosts.

Low-grade mobility: A mail relay or low-speed server can migrate to a different machine without invalidating cached addresses in DNS, by offloading addresses to peer machines within a subnet.

Merging subnets: Hosts that need to bridge logical networks can be assigned addresses on both, avoiding an extra routing hop.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mailroom: some addresses deliver packages, others deliver mail, others deliver bills. A firewall can let in mail but block packages. The address itself tells you who pays for delivery. Each worker gets their own mailbox for tracking work. A busy worker can pass their work address to a helper without changing records. Two offices can share one receiving desk with two addresses.

sections.title: Address Space Planning
sections.content:
The critical question is how many extra addresses to reserve per host. Most use cases require only a handful of addresses per system. Encoding services and billing policies each use a few addresses. Even per-user addressing is manageable if the number of concurrent users is reasonable.

However, Bellovin recommends reserving 2^6 (64) to 2^8 (256) extra addresses per host. This accounts for address mask assignment policies that allocate enough bits for the largest subnet in an organization, and provides headroom for networks to grow while keeping subnets contiguous. Sparse utilization of address space is an inevitable consequence of conservative planning.
sections.eli5: A big company might set aside 64 to 256 extra addresses per computer, just in case. It is better to reserve too many than to run out later and have to redesign everything.
